Chapter One: How Brands Became More Important Than Products
Think back for a second—maybe you remember when shopping was all about finding the thing that worked best, not the one with the most recognizable logo. But over time, something interesting happened. Business stopped focusing just on what they made, and started focusing on what they meant. That little logo? It used to just tell you where something came from. Now, it’s a symbol of a whole lifestyle.
In the late twentieth century, behind closed boardroom doors and bustling ad agencies, a quiet revolution was brewing. Leaders realized that just selling a product wasn’t enough anymore. They wanted to sell you an idea, a feeling, even a story. Suddenly, the logo took center stage, while the product itself slipped into the background. This shift went far beyond catchy ads or clever slogans. Brands began building entire worlds—where what mattered most was the meaning behind the name.
Imagine a teenager thumbing through a shiny magazine. At first, it might just look like a bunch of clothes, shoes, and gadgets. But soon, it’s clear: these aren’t just things to wear or use—they’re keys to fitting in, to feeling confident, to being cool. The right shoes? Suddenly, they’re about belonging to a tribe. That can of soda? It’s not just a drink; it’s a badge of identity. The message is everywhere: buy this, and you’ll be part of something bigger.
Meanwhile, companies started pouring more and more money into branding. The real action wasn’t happening in the factory anymore—it was in the design studios and marketing departments. The product itself? It could be made anywhere, by anyone. What really mattered was the story they told about it.
Maybe you’ve stood in a store, wondering why a simple T-shirt comes with such a hefty price tag. It’s rarely about the fabric. It’s about the logo on the chest, and the lifestyle it promises. Celebrity endorsements, splashy ad campaigns, all those carefully crafted images—they're baked right into the cost.
As brands grew more powerful, they started shaping more than just our shopping lists. They began to shape how we see ourselves. Picture a kid on a crowded schoolyard, feeling invisible without the right logo on their backpack. Or a young adult, looking for who they are, turning to brands for a little guidance. Suddenly, shopping wasn’t just about stuff—it was about showing the world your values, your dreams, even your rebellion.
But here’s something to pay attention to. As companies doubled down on branding, they started to step away from actually making the things they sold. Factories were moved overseas. Jobs disappeared. Communities that once depended on local manufacturing were left behind. The brand soared, while the people who made the products faded into the background.
At first, most of us didn’t even notice. The commercials were entertaining. The products felt familiar. Those logos? They almost seemed like old friends. But underneath it all, something new was taking hold—a kind of power that didn’t just shape what we buy, but how we live, work, and even see the world around us.
